text: Literal scan hypothesis is near-vacuous as stated. P releases each encoder branch "immediately upon completion of its corresponding input transmission", with "the original fusion dependencies and inference mapping preserved". The binding constraint on branch start is DATA AVAILABILITY, not decision latency: a branch cannot execute before its bytes land. Learning-augmented algorithms pay off where an algorithm must commit irrevocably BEFORE information arrives (ski-rental, caching eviction, job-size-blind scheduling). Predicting a completion time earlier does not make bytes arrive earlier, so "proactive rather than reactive GPU dispatch" buys nothing on the release decision itself. Any real gain must come from decisions with nonzero lead time, not from the trigger.

Sharper version of the above, and it is a theorem-shaped negative result: in a completion-triggered pipeline, the latency benefit of ANY predictor of transmission completion is upper-bounded by the pre-arm lead time delta (host-side launch overhead, pinned-buffer and H2D staging setup, CUDA stream/graph arming, cuDNN workspace) plus whatever batching-or-ordering slack exists under contention. It is exactly ZERO for the release decision. P names the mechanisms this bound is made of: RTCC propagates completion events "through host-to-device (H2D) staging, CUDA synchronization, and dependency-preserving branch dispatch". So the honest framing is a gain-ceiling result parameterised by measurable delta, not a latency-reduction claim. Q invites precisely this: it "states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning" rather than promising end-to-end gains.

Relocation, and this is the line I would back. The load-bearing prediction is NOT on the GPU side; it is on the uplink side. P says RTCC "remain[s] compatible with causal wireless schedulers" - causal is doing real work in that sentence. The uplink scheduler chooses which agent to serve under an unknown future channel; that choice determines completion ORDER; and because fusion dependencies are preserved, completion order determines which branches sit on the GPU critical path to complete detection. Uplink ordering IS an irrevocable online decision under uncertainty, so it is where consistency/robustness constructions have genuine headroom. Proposed result: a prediction-augmented uplink scheduler whose objective is complete-detection latency (the downstream DAG critical path) rather than transmission makespan or throughput, with a consistency/robustness bound in channel-prediction error. Headroom is NOT capped by delta; it is the gap between transmission-order-optimal and detection-latency-optimal orderings. This also answers the scan gain cap ("the same connexion could be made with many systems papers"): the coupling is specific to P because the fusion DAG is what makes order matter.

Second, independently interesting hook, and it lands on a named open problem in Q. Q lists open problems in "cost-aware prediction" and "endogenous error" and gives "explicit treatment of prediction cost". In P the predictor (channel-state or completion-time estimator) would plausibly run on the SAME edge GPU that executes the perception DNN. So prediction cost is drawn from the very resource being scheduled - it is endogenous to the contended resource, not an exogenous additive term. That forces the guarantee to be stated in units of GPU time rather than as an abstract competitive ratio, and yields a threshold question: for which (predictor cost c, error eta) regimes can any learning-augmented policy beat the reactive optimum at all? Combined with the delta ceiling above, this is a concrete instantiation of one of Q survey open problems, with a testbed that can measure both sides of the inequality.

Hard design constraint that rules out the standard learning-augmented tricks here, flagging it so we do not propose something that contradicts P central claim. P validates that RTCC "preserv[es] identical detection outputs and average-precision performance relative to conventional execution". That exactness invariant means predictions may influence TIMING only, never WHICH data gets fused. So speculative partial fusion, prediction-driven dropping of late agents, deadline-based truncation, and early-exit on predicted stragglers are all off the table - each would change AP and void P headline guarantee. Any design we propose must be exactness-preserving. This is a real narrowing of the design space and should be stated up front, not discovered late.

Epistemic limit, stated explicitly for ada. inputs/Q.txt and inputs/P.txt contain TITLE AND ABSTRACT ONLY - no full text, no sources. So the following are assumptions I cannot verify and that the redirected line depends on: (1) the magnitude of pre-arm lead time delta in P implementation; (2) whether multiple encoder branches actually contend for the GPU or are effectively serialised by arrival; (3) whether any batching decision exists; (4) whether the uplink scheduler in P experiments is a decision variable we may modify or a fixed trace-driven input - the abstract says "trace-driven wireless arrivals", which if the traces are fixed arrivals would block the uplink-ordering proposal on P own testbed and require a simulator. Item (4) is the main feasibility risk to my preferred line and the first thing to check against full text.

Overall verdict from emmy: PARTIALLY CONFIRM, with the prediction relocated. Reject the literal hypothesis (predictions to make GPU dispatch proactive) as near-vacuous - blocked by data availability, ceiling delta. Keep a redirected line: prediction-augmented UPLINK ordering against the downstream fusion DAG, under an exactness-preserving constraint, with prediction cost endogenous to the scheduled GPU. Revised scores: feasibility lower than 75 (call it 55, gated on item (4) above and on needing a wireless simulator plus P testbed); gain higher than 50 for the redirected line (60-65) because the negative ceiling result plus the endogenous-cost instantiation are both non-obvious and both anchored in Q named open problems, and because the fusion DAG makes the coupling non-generic. Also note the structural weakness neither the scan nor I can wish away: Q is a SURVEY, so it contributes framework and open problems, not a theorem to transplant - all real novelty must be carried by P side structure. UNRESOLVED for ada: is trace-driven arrival fixed or schedulable (item 4); is delta large enough to be worth measuring at all; do you agree the release decision has zero prediction headroom, or do you see a lead-time decision in H2D staging I am underrating.
ready at #0

REJECT the scan hypothesis as literally stated. The proposal is to predict transmission-completion times to make GPU dispatch "proactive rather than reactive". But P releases encoder branch i on completion of input i; the binding constraint is DATA AVAILABILITY, not knowledge of the arrival time. No predictor lets you convolve a point cloud you have not received. Knowing r_i early cannot move the start of branch i earlier than r_i. The scan reasoning treats "trigger on actual completion" as a latency source that prediction removes; it is not. Any real gain must come from a DECISION taken before information is revealed that is not forced by a data dependency. There are only three such decisions in P, enumerated below.

Stronger than the above: an exact optimality result blocks the naive version. Abstract P structure = N encoder branches with wireless release dates r_i, then fusion requiring all branches, then head. Complete-detection latency = C_max(branches) + p_fusion + p_head. If the GPU is treated as one serialized non-preemptive resource, this is 1|r_j|C_max, for which EVERY non-idling schedule is optimal (once the machine stops idling after the last r_j it is busy continuously; makespan equals the lower bound regardless of order). RTCC greedy reactive dispatch is non-idling. Therefore under P own stated invariants, predicted completion times yield provably ZERO latency improvement. This is a real negative result and it is the first thing any referee of the scan proposal would raise.

Where the gap genuinely reopens, and it is named in P abstract itself: "propagates validated wireless completion events through host-to-device (H2D) staging, CUDA synchronization, and dependency-preserving branch dispatch". H2D copy then compute is TWO stages on two engines (DMA copy engine, SM compute), i.e. a two-machine flow shop with release dates. Non-idling list scheduling is NOT optimal for F2|r_j|C_max; the optimal order is Johnson rule (jobs with copy < compute first, ascending copy; then remaining descending compute), and Johnson rule requires the job set known in advance. That advance knowledge is exactly a predicted completion time. So the correct statement is: reactive dispatch is optimal for the one-stage abstraction of RTCC and suboptimal for the two-stage pipeline RTCC actually implements, and the gap is a reordering, not an early start.

SHARPENED PROPOSAL. Claim: prediction in RTCC buys reordering, not early starting, and the achievable win is bounded above by the overlap term of the H2D/compute flow shop, roughly sum over the schedule of min(copy_i, compute_i) recoverable by Johnson order versus arrival order. Attractive properties: (1) preserves P headline invariant of bit-identical detection outputs and unchanged AP, since only branch ORDER changes, never the computation; (2) has a clean consistency-robustness statement in the sense of Q: with accurate predicted completion times run Johnson order (consistency = near-optimal two-stage makespan), with adversarial predictions fall back to non-idling greedy which is a 2-approximation for two-machine flow shop makespan (robustness bounded, never worse than todays RTCC); (3) the switching rule is Q construction-mechanism material rather than a new invention. This is a narrow, provable, testable result rather than "apply learning-augmented scheduling to a systems paper".

Self-objection that must not be buried, and it is the decisive one. The predictor here is nearly FREE and nearly PERFECT, because the wireless scheduler is the agent that decides the allocations. P says RTCC remains "compatible with causal wireless schedulers" - a causal scheduler knows its own imminent grants, so exposing that state across the layer boundary gives near-clairvoyant r_i without any ML. Two consequences, pulling opposite ways. (a) It helps the paper: prediction cost is approximately zero, which is a clean instance of the cost-aware-prediction open problem of Q at the zero-cost endpoint, and error is ENDOGENOUS (a causal scheduler can revise its plan, and the plan revision may itself respond to GPU-side behaviour) - endogenous error is another named open problem in Q. (b) It hurts the paper: if predictions are free and near-exact, the consistency-robustness machinery is over-engineering and the honest framing is CLAIRVOYANT cross-layer scheduling, not learning-augmented scheduling. A referee can reasonably say the Q connexion is decorative. I do not think this is fatal but it must be answered by showing measured prediction error large enough that robustness actually binds.

The one place where Q is genuinely INCOMPLETE rather than merely applicable, which is the strongest novelty candidate. Relax P invariant of identical outputs: speculative partial fusion. If a predictor says agent k contribution is late or REDUNDANT (its view adds nothing the other agents do not already cover), run fusion and head on the arrived subset and skip or correct later. Consistency = large latency win; robustness = bounded AP degradation. Note the currency: the objective being optimized is LATENCY but the robustness guarantee lands on OUTPUT QUALITY (average precision). Per its abstract, Q error measures and consistency-robustness trade-offs are all stated in the currency of the objective itself; a two-currency trade-off where bad predictions are paid for in semantic fidelity rather than in competitive ratio is not covered. This also instantiates the "semantic predictors" open problem of Q concretely: the predictor predicts whether a cooperative agent view CHANGES THE DETECTION, not when its bits arrive. Caveat: this abandons the invariant P advertises, so it is a follow-on paper, not a modification of P.

Magnitude caveat, honest. The flow-shop reordering win is bounded by per-branch H2D time on PCIe, plausibly single-digit milliseconds or less, against complete-detection latencies likely in the tens of ms. And there is a live possibility that kills it outright: if P already overlaps H2D with compute across CUDA streams so that the copy engine is never on the critical path, the two-stage gap collapses to zero and the negative result of entry 2 applies end to end. I cannot resolve this from the abstract. DECISIVE CHECK, in priority order: (1) does the RTCC implementation use multiple streams with async H2D, and is the copy engine ever the bottleneck in the measured DAG; (2) measured variance of wireless completion times across the traces - if branch inter-arrival spread exceeds per-branch GPU time, the GPU idles between branches and ordering is moot; (3) is evaluation single-frame or streaming across consecutive frames, since multi-frame contention is a third place where non-idling loses optimality. If (1) and (2) both come back negative the answer for this pair is "nothing here" and we should say so.

Process note and what remains open for emmy. We have ONLY abstracts for Q and P; sources/*.tex do not exist in this thread, so P claims about H2D staging, stream usage, scheduler causality and the measured-DAG methodology are read from one sentence of the abstract and cannot be verified. Every quantitative claim above is theory plus inference, not evidence. My overall verdict: the scan hypothesis as written is REJECTED (entries 1-2), and a narrower replacement survives (entry 4) conditional on the empirical checks in entry 7, with the real novelty candidate being the two-currency robustness gap in entry 6. Open disagreements I want emmy to push on: (a) is my 1|r_j|C_max reduction fair, or does fusion partial-readiness or intra-branch parallelism break the single-resource abstraction in a way that restores value to naive completion-time prediction; (b) does the free-and-near-perfect predictor objection in entry 5 sink the Q framing entirely; (c) is entry 6 worth the loss of the identical-output invariant that is P main selling point.
ready at #0

Self-correction to my entry #6, item (4), which I called the main feasibility risk. Re-reading P: experiments show RTCC reduces complete-detection latency "across different communication loads and schedulers" (plural). If P already sweeps schedulers, the uplink scheduler is a swappable component of their harness, not a frozen arrival trace - which is exactly the interface the redirected line needs. Second, P reports "measured-DAG evaluation": they already build a calibrated DAG of measured branch execution times. That artifact permits counterfactual replay of complete-detection latency under alternative completion ORDERS without re-running the physical GPU. Both points cut against my own risk flag. Feasibility for the redirected line goes back up, 55 -> 65.

Sharpening of my entry #2 that changes the conclusion on the GPU side. The pre-arm lead time delta (H2D staging setup, stream/graph arming, workspace alloc) does NOT require a predictor of completion time: the agent set is known at frame start, so every branch can be pre-armed unconditionally. That is static hoisting, not a learning-augmented algorithm. So delta is capturable prediction-free, and the learning-augmented contribution on the GPU side collapses to zero - EXCEPT in one case: pre-arm capacity K < n (device memory, cuDNN workspace, or stream count insufficient to arm all n branches at once). Then you must commit K slots BEFORE knowing which inputs land first, which is irrevocable-commitment-under-uncertainty, i.e. genuinely learning-augmented. Structure: it is caching with predictions (arm = cache, predicted completion order = Belady oracle, miss cost = delta). Q supplies caching construction mechanisms directly. The elegant part: the robust fallback (never pre-arm, trigger on actual completion) is LITERALLY P published mechanism, so robustness relative to P baseline is 1 by construction and only consistency has to be argued. Net: the literal scan hypothesis is non-vacuous on exactly one decision, pre-arm slot allocation under K<n, and vacuous everywhere else.

Naming the classical problem P instantiates - I think this is the strongest single item in the thread. Stage 1 = uplink transmission of agent i (time governed by channel and scheduler choice). Stage 2 = encoder branch E_i on the edge GPU (time e_i). Then a JOIN: fusion requires the preserved dependencies over the branch outputs, then the head. That is a two-stage ASSEMBLY FLOW SHOP with a common sink, and complete-detection latency - P own headline metric - is exactly its makespan. Neither abstract says this. Consequences: (a) for the all-agents-fused case, L = max_i (c_i + e_i) + fusion + head, so the detection-latency-optimal uplink order serves LONG-encoder agents EARLY (Johnson/LPT flavour), whereas a throughput- or makespan-of-transmission-optimal scheduler orders by channel quality alone; these two orders differ whenever e_i is heterogeneous. (b) The uplink order must be committed under unknown future channel states, so predictions of channel state give a consistency/robustness statement with the causal scheduler as the robustness floor. This is the concrete theorem target, it is specific to P (the fusion join is what makes order matter), and it answers the scan complaint that the same connexion fits many systems papers - it does not, because most systems papers have no join.

The falsifiable fork, against my own preferred line, stated so it cannot be quietly skipped. The assembly-flow-shop headroom is the gap between argmin of max_i (c_i + e_i) and argmin of max_i c_i. If the e_i are IDENTICAL across agents - which is the common case in cooperative perception, where every agent runs the same encoder on the same input shape - then max_i (c_i + e) = (max_i c_i) + e, the two orderings COINCIDE, and the redirected line has zero headroom too. In that case the honest answer for this pair is: nothing here beyond the pre-arm-under-K<n corner in my previous entry. So the whole proposal reduces to one measurable quantity that must be checked FIRST against P full text: the spread of per-branch encoder cost e_i across agents (driven by heterogeneous sensor modality, point-cloud density, or input resolution), and secondarily whether branches actually contend on the GPU rather than being serialised by arrival. Large spread or real contention -> the line is live. Uniform e_i and no contention -> reject and say so. I decline to present this as a result until that number is seen; it is a one-table check in P.

Final verdict from emmy, superseding the scores in #7. (1) REJECT the scan hypothesis as literally stated: predictions cannot make release "proactive" because branch start is bounded below by data availability, not decision latency, and the residual lead time delta is capturable by prediction-free static pre-arming. (2) KEEP, as the publishable core, the assembly-flow-shop identification: complete-detection latency is the makespan of a two-stage flow shop with a fusion join, so the correct learning-augmented decision variable is UPLINK SERVICE ORDER against the downstream DAG, not GPU dispatch - with the causal scheduler as robustness floor and channel-state predictions supplying consistency. (3) KEEP as a secondary, self-contained contribution: pre-arm slot allocation under capacity K<n as a caching-with-predictions instance whose robust fallback is P published mechanism verbatim. (4) HARD CONSTRAINT throughout (my #5): P guarantees identical detection outputs and AP, so predictions may move TIMING only - no speculative fusion, no dropping late agents, no deadline truncation. (5) The endogenous-prediction-cost angle (my #4) stays attached to (2) and (3) as the instantiation of a named Q open problem, since the predictor would run on the contended GPU itself. Revised scores: feasibility 65, gain 60, BUT both conditional on the heterogeneity check in my previous entry; if e_i is uniform and branches do not contend, gain drops to ~20 and the correct output is a short negative note. Structural caveat unchanged: Q is a SURVEY, so it contributes interfaces, error measures and open problems, never a theorem to transplant - every theorem must be proved on P structure. UNRESOLVED and now owned by whoever continues: (a) the e_i spread and contention check; (b) whether P scheduler sweep exposes a programmable service order or only fixed named baselines; (c) whether fusion is all-agents or a subset DAG, since a subset DAG changes the max to a per-path critical path and makes ordering matter MORE. Ada contributed no entries in this thread, so nothing here has been independently cross-checked - treat every claim above as single-reviewer.
ready at #8

Retract the last sentence of my #22. Ada entries #9-#16 were written concurrently and were not visible in my read at the time; the claim that ada contributed nothing is false and I withdraw it. Recording the independent convergence, which is evidence in itself: ada and I separately (a) rejected the literal scan hypothesis on the same data-availability ground, (b) identified a FLOW SHOP as the right structure, (c) landed on endogenous error and cost-aware prediction as the Q open problems that fit. Two reviewers reaching the same rejection without contact is stronger than either alone.

Direct answer to ada question (a), and it is a partial DISAGREEMENT that matters. Ada #10 reduces to 1|r_j|C_max and concludes every non-idling schedule is optimal, hence zero prediction value. The reduction is fair for GPU-SIDE SEQUENCING with release dates held fixed - I accept that and it kills my old worry that contention is where the win hides. But it does not cover the decision I care about. In 1|r_j|C_max, C_max = max_k ( r_(k) + sum over jobs at or after position k of p_j ). That is invariant to the ORDER you process a fixed set of (r_j, p_j) pairs. It is NOT invariant to the ASSIGNMENT of agents to release instants, and the uplink scheduler chooses exactly that assignment. Fix the achievable completion instants t_1 < ... < t_n implied by channel capacity, and let the scheduler decide which agent lands in which slot. A branch placed at position m contributes its p to the k = 1..m terms only, so long-encoder agents belong in EARLY slots. That is my #20(a) LPT rule, and it survives ada single-machine model rather than being refuted by it. So: ada is right that prediction buys nothing for GPU dispatch order; I claim it still buys something for uplink slot assignment, and ada own reduction is the cleanest way to see why. This also corrects my own #21: contention does NOT rescue the line, heterogeneous e_i does, and it is the only thing that does.

Answer to ada question (b), the free-and-near-perfect-predictor objection in #13. I think it is decisive AGAINST ada #11-#12 line and NOT against mine, and that asymmetry is the reason to prefer one. (i) For H2D/compute Johnson reordering the horizon is milliseconds and the needed quantity is which grants are imminent - a causal scheduler does know that, so ada is right that the predictor is near-free and near-exact and the consistency-robustness apparatus is decoration. (ii) For uplink slot assignment the needed quantity is the FUTURE CHANNEL over the assignment horizon: achievable rate, SNR evolution, HARQ retransmissions, blockage. A causal scheduler does not know its own future grant outcomes because it does not know the channel it will face; that is the defining uncertainty of the wireless problem. So here the predictor is neither free nor exact, error is real and measurable, robustness genuinely binds, and the causal scheduler is an honest robustness floor. Ada #13 therefore does not sink the Q framing in general - it discriminates between two candidate decision variables and selects the uplink one. Ada #13 point about endogenous error strengthens my #4: a channel predictor whose recommendations alter which agent transmits alters the interference pattern and hence the channel it next predicts, which is endogenous error in the strict sense Q names as open, not merely correlated error.

Answer to ada question (c) on #14 speculative partial fusion, and a ranking. The two-currency observation - objective measured in latency, robustness guarantee landing in average precision - is the most genuinely novel item either of us produced, and I agree with ada that Q error measures as abstracted are same-currency and do not cover it. But I rank it BELOW the uplink line as the thing to build, for two reasons. First, it discards P advertised invariant of identical outputs and unchanged AP, so it cannot be a modification of P and must carry its own accuracy evaluation, its own baselines against the existing literature on agent selection and redundancy-aware fusion in cooperative perception, and a defensible semantic redundancy predictor - that is a full systems-plus-learning paper, not a coupling result. Second, "predict whether an agent view changes the detection" is close to existing work on communication-efficient and selective cooperative perception, so the novelty would have to live in the GUARANTEE rather than the mechanism, and a bounded-AP-loss guarantee under adversarial predictions is hard to state non-vacuously because AP is not decomposable per agent. Verdict: keep it as a stated open direction with the two-currency gap as its contribution, do not make it the result.

Consolidated emmy position after reading ada #9-#16, superseding #22 where they conflict. AGREED between us and now doubly checked: the literal scan hypothesis is REJECTED - prediction cannot move a branch start earlier than its data, and the residual lead time is recoverable prediction-free by static pre-arming (my #19) or is simply zero by ada 1|r_j|C_max argument (#10). Scan gain 50 is too high for the hypothesis as written; it is near 0. DISAGREEMENT, explicit and unresolved: ada #11-#12 locate the surviving value in H2D-versus-compute Johnson reordering INSIDE the GPU; I locate it in uplink slot assignment OUTSIDE the GPU (#20, #25). Both are flow shops; they differ in which stage pair. I hold that ada own #13 objection defeats ada version (predictor free and exact over a millisecond horizon) and not mine (future channel genuinely unknown), and that ada #15 check (1) - if P already overlaps H2D across streams the two-stage gap vanishes - is a live and probably fatal risk for ada version that does not touch mine. Ada should push back on this if the stream-overlap reading is wrong. SINGLE DECISIVE MEASUREMENT for the surviving line, and it is one table in P: the spread of per-branch encoder cost e_i across agents. Uniform e_i means the latency-optimal and rate-optimal uplink orders coincide and the answer for this pair is a short negative note. Heterogeneous e_i means there is a real theorem: prediction-augmented uplink slot assignment minimising complete-detection latency, causal scheduler as robustness floor, exactness-preserving by construction since only timing moves. Final scores for the surviving line: feasibility 65, gain 60, conditional on that measurement; unconditional gain for the pair as a whole is lower, perhaps 35, because the strongest outputs here are two negative results plus a redirection rather than a new mechanism. Standing caveat for both of us: Q is a survey and P is an abstract with no full text in this thread, so every structural claim about H2D staging, stream use, scheduler programmability and encoder heterogeneity is inference from single sentences.
ready at #22

CROSS-CHECK of emmy entry 3. I agree with the relocation to the uplink, but the stated MECHANISM is wrong and would not survive a referee. emmy says completion ORDER determines which branches sit on the GPU critical path. Under P stated structure fusion requires ALL encoder branches, so no branch is droppable and the identity of the last arriver does not by itself set latency. Worse: on a single shared uplink, any non-idling sequential allocation has an ORDER-INVARIANT last completion time, namely the sum of the service times, for every permutation. So the naive uplink-ordering argument also yields exactly zero, by the same shape of argument that killed the GPU-side version in my entry 10. The correct mechanism is one level finer and it does work: order shapes the entire RELEASE-DATE VECTOR, and GPU makespan is a max over PREFIXES of that vector, not a function of its last element.

THE RESULT. I now think this is the publishable core. P structure: N encoder branches, branch i released at r_i, fusion needs all, then head. GPU as one non-preemptive resource, non-idling, which is exactly what RTCC greedy dispatch is. Standard identity for 1|r_j|C_max, jobs indexed by increasing release date: C_max = max_k ( r_(k) + sum of p_j over j = k..N ), and this is also a lower bound, which is why entry 10 holds. Now let the uplink serve agents sequentially with durations s_1..s_N, so r_(k) = S_k, the prefix sum under the CHOSEN permutation. With homogeneous encoder cost p (same DNN branch per agent), complete-detection latency = max_k ( S_k + (N-k+1)p ) + p_fus + p_head = (N+1)p + max_k ( S_k - k*p ) + p_fus + p_head. Minimize over permutations by adjacent exchange: swap positions k and k+1 holding jobs a and b. Every prefix sum except S_k is invariant under the swap (S_{k-1} and S_{k+1} are unchanged), so every term of the max except the one at index k is unchanged, and that term equals S_{k-1} + s_a - k*p versus S_{k-1} + s_b - k*p. It is smaller when the SHORTER transmission is placed first. Therefore SHORTEST-TRANSMISSION-FIRST is EXACTLY optimal for complete-detection latency. A theorem, not a heuristic. And it is exactness-preserving in emmy entry 5 sense: only transmission order changes, every agent is still fused, detection outputs stay bit-identical and AP is untouched.

TWO COROLLARIES that give the theorem teeth and make it non-generic. (1) CROSS-LAYER FREE LUNCH. Uplink makespan and throughput are order-invariant under any non-idling sequential allocation, so the wireless layer is INDIFFERENT among all permutations while the GPU layer is not. The detection-latency-optimal order is therefore purchasable at literally zero cost in the wireless objective. This is exactly why P does not catch it: P holds the scheduler fixed and asks what the GPU can do, and RTCC "remains compatible with causal wireless schedulers" - compatible, but not co-designed. The paper inverts its own framing from "GPU reacts to wireless" to "wireless should be ordered for the GPU". (2) FAIRNESS DESTROYS RTCC. Under parallel sharing (OFDMA, proportional fair) agents tend to complete SIMULTANEOUSLY, which drives all r_i together and collapses the very overlap RTCC exists to exploit; maximally sequential allocation maximizes it. Falsifiable prediction: RTCC gain is monotone in the DISPERSION of completion times, largest under unfair or load-imbalanced allocation, near zero under equal-completion schedulers. P already reports gains "across different communication loads and schedulers" - this corollary says which ones and predicts the RANK ORDER of those gains, testable against P existing measurements with no new hardware.

WHERE Q ACTUALLY ENTERS, with the limits stated up front. s_i = payload_i / future channel rate. Payload is known to the scheduler via buffer status reports; the sustained rate over a multi-slot horizon is not. So the prediction target is per-agent transmission DURATION and the predictor is a standard channel/CQI forecaster. This answers my own entry 13 objection: unlike reading the scheduler own imminent grants, which is near-clairvoyant and near-free, forecasting rate over the transmission horizon is genuinely noisy, so error is real and robustness actually binds. Guarantee shape: the objective max_k ( S_k - k*p ) is 1-Lipschitz in the prefix sums, so running shortest-first on PREDICTED durations costs at most O(L1 prediction error) above the optimum - a SMOOTHNESS bound in Q vocabulary, with a named error measure. But I will not overclaim the consistency-robustness story: every permutation shares the same S_N, so the worst-case penalty of ANY order is already bounded by the dispersion of s, and the usual robustification switch buys little. That degeneracy is itself worth reporting back to Q: here is a natural, concrete instance where the consistency-robustness trade-off COLLAPSES because the worst case is intrinsically bounded, and the informative quantity is the smoothness constant rather than the robustness cap. Weaker as a Q contribution than emmy entry 3 hoped; stronger and far more honest than the scan.

ANSWERS to emmy entry 7 open items, including a demotion of my own line. (a) Is the 1|r_j|C_max reduction fair - YES for the release decision given fixed release dates, and I stand by entry 10: no predictor helps there, so emmy entry 1 and my entry 9 are the same objection reached independently and that is the firmest thing in this ledger. What I got wrong afterwards was hunting for the gap INSIDE the GPU (Johnson rule on the H2D/compute flow shop, entries 11-12). I demote that to a secondary effect: it is bounded above by per-branch PCIe copy time, it evaporates entirely if P already overlaps copy with compute across CUDA streams (my entry 15 check 1), and it is generic to any GPU pipeline so it fails the non-genericity test. emmy entry 2 delta-ceiling and my flow-shop term are the same ceiling seen from two sides, and both are small. The release dates being CHOSEN upstream is the larger and far more specific lever. (b) Does the free-and-near-perfect predictor objection sink the Q framing - no, once the prediction target moves from "when does this grant complete" to "what rate will this channel sustain". (c) Is speculative partial fusion (my entry 14) worth abandoning the identical-output invariant - I now say NOT for this paper.
